slides: Open the lecture by naming the central habit of the chapter: do not trust the Euclidean drawing until the model has been identified. Elliptic and hyperbolic geometry are presented here through quotients, projective balls, conformal disks, distance formulas, isometries, and measure, so the class should keep asking which features are intrinsic.

Use the route slide as a contract with the audience. Each row pairs a model choice with an invariant check, so students know that straight chords, circular arcs, antipodal lifts, and boundary blow-up are not separate topics. They are different tests for separating geometry from coordinates.

Spend time on the absolute value in the elliptic distance formula. It is not a trick added for convenience; it is the metric trace of identifying antipodal unit vectors. The displayed artifact lets students compare the spherical separation of opposite lifts with zero elliptic distance in the quotient.

This slide gives the elliptic side a projective grammar. Points are lines through the origin, lines are planes through the origin after quotienting, and isometries descend from orthogonal transformations. Emphasize that many familiar spherical pictures double-count data until the antipodal identification is enforced.

Introduce the Klein ball as the first hyperbolic model because it keeps projective straightness visible. The cost is that Euclidean angles are not reliable. The distance formula should be read as a cross-ratio or Lorentz-form invariant rather than as a function of ordinary chord length.

Make the coordinate change concrete: the same hyperbolic line is a straight chord in Klein coordinates and a boundary-orthogonal circular arc in Poincare coordinates. Ask students to inspect the artifact for what changed and then point to the residuals showing that distance and orthogonality survived.

Frame the Poincare disk as the angle-friendly model, not the universally truthful model. It preserves conformal angle information but still distorts Euclidean size severely near the boundary. The distance formula and the boundary-growth artifact together explain why visual nearness to the rim means hyperbolic remoteness.

Treat disk automorphisms as the working laboratory for hyperbolic isometries. Points visibly move, Euclidean side lengths change, and the triangle is redrawn, but the hyperbolic pairwise distances agree to numerical precision. This is the clearest place to distinguish motion in a picture from motion in the geometry.

Use the comparison table to slow down common misconceptions. A line, angle, distance, and area can each be easy in one model and awkward in another. Students should leave this slide with a decision procedure: choose the model that makes the invariant under discussion easiest to inspect.

Connect measure to the earlier boundary warnings. The density formulas look different in Klein and Poincare coordinates because they are written against different Euclidean area elements. The agreement as a function of hyperbolic radius is the invariant fact, and the large area values are not drawing errors.

Bring the projective and conformal stories back to transformations. Elliptic isometries arise from orthogonal transformations modulo the antipodal ambiguity, while hyperbolic projective isometries preserve the boundary quadric. In the disk, the same symmetry appears as a fractional-linear transformation preserving the unit disk.

Use the worked diagnostic as a model for student computations. Start with a visible coordinate picture, compute an intrinsic quantity, change the model or apply an isometry, and check that the intrinsic quantity is unchanged. The point is not numerical decoration; it is a proof habit.

Close by collecting the lecture into four reusable tests. Quotient tests handle elliptic ambiguity, model-change tests handle Klein and Poincare drawings, isometry tests handle transformations, and measure tests handle boundary growth. The final message is that models are tools, while invariants carry the geometry.
